```{python}
# `connected=False` embeds DataTables rather than fetching it from a CDN, so
# the published page has no external dependency and works offline. It costs
# about 200 kB, and only this page uses it.
init_notebook_mode(all_interactive=False, connected=False)


def table(df, page=25, order=None):
    """A sortable, searchable ranking table.

    Not `display(df)`: pandas caps its HTML repr at 60 rows, which silently
    truncated the 355-row Tier B ranking to the first 60 -- a ranking that
    stops two thirds of the way down, with nothing on the page saying so.
    """
    # `allow_html=True` is required for the ICAO column: without it itables
    # escapes the anchor tags and the reader sees the raw `<a href=...>` markup
    # as text in the cell, with nothing clickable.
    ishow(df, maxBytes=0, lengthMenu=[25, 50, 100, 500],
          pageLength=page, scrollX=True, allow_html=True,
          order=order if order is not None else [],
          classes="display compact")

HAVE = bool(_data.periods_available())
LATEST = _data.latest() if HAVE else None
```

```{python}
**The question this page answers:** when an aircraft moves at a European
airport, how much of that movement does OpenSky's receiver network actually
see?

Not much, at many of them. A flight is nearly always spotted *somewhere* —
detection runs above 99% almost everywhere — but being spotted once in the air
is very different from being tracked across the apron and down the runway. The
ranking below is built on the second question, because that is the one that
decides whether ground events can be derived at all.
```

## The fleet

```{python}
#| echo: false
if HAVE:
    a = _data.load_ranking("a", LATEST)
    b = _data.load_ranking("b", LATEST)

    def _summary(s, label, pct=False):
        s = pd.Series(s).dropna()
        if s.empty:
            return {"metric": label, "n": 0}
        f = (lambda v: f"{v:.1f}%") if pct else (lambda v: f"{v:.3f}")
        return {
            "metric": label, "n": len(s),
            "median": f(s.median()),
            "IQR": f"{f(s.quantile(.25))} – {f(s.quantile(.75))}",
            "p10": f(s.quantile(.10)), "p90": f(s.quantile(.90)),
        }

    display(Markdown(
        "Where the aerodromes sit as a group, before looking at any one of "
        "them. Each row is one measure; the columns are its spread across "
        "aerodromes — the middle value, the middle half, and the worst and "
        "best tenths. A median of 100% for “seen” with a much lower median "
        "for “received” is the whole finding of this site in two lines: "
        "aircraft are almost always spotted, and often barely tracked."
    ))
    display(Markdown(explain_block(
        ["detection_pct", "signal_p50", "coverage_index"],
        title="What these measures are",
    )))
    # Plain labels, and the same measures the tables below use. This showed
    # bin occupancy under the word "observed" and a reach row that appears
    # nowhere else on the site -- both left over from earlier versions.
    rows = [
        _summary(b.detection_pct, "Flights seen — all aerodromes", pct=True),
        _summary(a.detection_pct, "Flights seen — aerodromes with measured "
                                  "times", pct=True),
        _summary(a.dep_signal_p50, "Taxi-out received — measured aerodromes"),
        _summary(a.arr_signal_p50, "Taxi-in received — measured aerodromes"),
        _summary(a.coverage_index, "Coverage index — measured aerodromes"),
    ]
    display(pd.DataFrame(rows))
```

## Ground coverage — aerodromes with measured times

```{python}
#| echo: false
if HAVE:
    display(Markdown(
        f"{len(a)} aerodromes where APDF measures all four milestones, so ground "
        f"capture is computable. Ranked on `coverage_index` = "
        f"`detection_rate x mean(dep_signal_p50, arr_signal_p50)`, best first."
    ))
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
if HAVE:
    # Six columns and a rating. The earlier eleven made it slow to find the
    # well- and badly-covered aerodromes, which is the one thing this table
    # exists for; the rest moved to the aerodrome pages.
    t = a.copy()
    t["signal_p50"] = t[["dep_signal_p50", "arr_signal_p50"]].mean(axis=1)
    t["rating"] = [rating(v) for v in t["coverage_index"]]
    # Fragmented and merged combined into one column. Both are tracking
    # errors and both depress coverage; which of the two it is matters when
    # diagnosing an aerodrome, and that breakdown is on its own page. Two
    # columns here would buy that distinction at the cost of the scannability
    # this table was trimmed for.
    t["tracking_err_pct"] = (t["fragmented_pct_dep"].fillna(0)
                             + t["merged_pct_dep"].fillna(0))
    cols = ["rank", "icao", "name", "n_gt", "detection_pct", "signal_p50",
            "coverage_index", "rating", "tracking_err_pct"]
    t = t[[c for c in cols if c in t.columns]]
    t["detection_pct"] = t["detection_pct"].round(1)
    for c in ("signal_p50", "coverage_index"):
        t[c] = t[c].round(3)
    t["tracking_err_pct"] = t["tracking_err_pct"].round(1)
    t["n_gt"] = t["n_gt"].astype("Int64")
    display(Markdown(explain_block(cols)))
    t["icao"] = [f'<a href="airports/{i}.html">{i}</a>' for i in t["icao"]]
    table(rename(t))
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
if HAVE:
    # The estimated taxi-out is carried only where there is no measured one,
    # so the column cannot be read as a second opinion on an aerodrome that
    # already has the real figure -- the two are computed against different
    # windows and are not comparable side by side.
    b = b.copy()
    b["dep_signal_est"] = b["dep_signal_p50"].where(b["measured"] == "no")
    cols = ["rank", "icao", "name", "n_gt", "detection_pct", "measured",
            "off_s_p50", "land_s_p50", "dep_signal_est"]
    t = b[[c for c in cols if c in b.columns]].copy()
    t["dep_signal_est"] = t["dep_signal_est"].round(3)
    t["detection_pct"] = t["detection_pct"].round(1)
    for c in ("off_s_p50", "land_s_p50"):
        if c in t:
            t[c] = t[c].round(0).astype("Int64")
    t["n_gt"] = t["n_gt"].astype("Int64")
    display(Markdown(explain_block(cols)))
    t["icao"] = [f'<a href="airports/{i}.html">{i}</a>' for i in t["icao"]]
    table(rename(t))
```

## What "coverage" means here

Two different questions, and the difference between them is the point.

**Was the flight seen at all?** One position report anywhere between take-off
and landing is enough. Answerable at every aerodrome, and almost everywhere in
Europe the answer is "yes, above 99% of the time".

**How much of its time on the ground was received?** The taxi is bounded by
real stand and runway times, the feed should deliver a report every 5 seconds,
and we count how many of those expected reports actually arrived. Answerable
only where those times are recorded — and the answer varies enormously.

The coverage index multiplies the two. An aerodrome can score 99% on the first
and near zero on the second, and several do: the aircraft is tracked in the
air and invisible on the ground.

Between those two questions sits a third. Network Manager predicts a taxi
duration for every European departure, and that prediction is unbiased even
though it is loose — so for an aerodrome with no measured times, the *median*
share of its taxi-out that arrived can still be estimated. That figure is the
last column of the second table. Nothing equivalent exists for arrivals: no
in-block time is recorded outside APDF, so there is no window to measure a
taxi-in against, and the index — which needs both — stays a Tier A number.

## What the ranking does not say

- An aerodrome outside the ingested area is **absent**, not ranked last — see
  the map above. Its movements were never sampled, so any figure for it would
  measure the boundary rather than the receiver network. Flights *to* those
  aerodromes still count at their European end.
- **A low coverage index has two possible causes, and they need different
  fixes.** Position reports arrive as one continuous stream per aircraft, with
  nothing in them marking where one flight ends and the next begins, so the
  flights have to be cut out of that stream first. When the cut goes wrong,
  coverage looks worse than the receivers deserve:

  - *split* — one flight cut into several tracks. Coverage is measured against
    the largest piece, so the rest of the flight is not counted and the
    aerodrome is understated.
  - *merged* — two flights left in one track. The worse failure: only one
    flight comes out, so the other does not exist downstream at all.

  The **tracking errors** column adds the two together, as a share of that
  aerodrome's movements. A high figure means read its coverage with caution.
  Each aerodrome's page breaks it into split and merged separately, which is
  the distinction that matters when diagnosing one.
- The two tiers are not comparable and are never merged into one table.
